title: A new 1 TiB ext4 filesystem lets users write 93% of it; the 5% root reserve is nearly three times all its metadata

steps.title: mkfs.ext4 makes 1 GiB into 262,144 blocks of 4 KiB
steps.line: 5.0% of the blocks hold metadata before any file is written.
steps.caption: mke2fs.conf sets 4096-byte blocks, so 1 GiB is 262,144 blocks in 8 groups of 32,768. Before any file is written, 13,019 blocks, 5.0%, already hold metadata: the filesystem’s own structures. The pie counts blocks as dumpe2fs reports them after a real mkfs.ext4 run. The question is how much of this new disk a regular user can write: metadata consumes blocks now, while the root and kernel reserves hold back some of the remaining free blocks.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 1 GiB”: 2 slices; “After mkfs.ext4”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: Inode tables are 31.5% of the metadata
steps.line: One 256-byte inode per 16 KiB of disk: 65,536 inodes.
steps.caption: This pie’s whole is the 13,019 metadata blocks. mke2fs makes one inode per 16 KiB of disk from 512 MiB to under 4 TiB, per 32 KiB to under 16 TiB, and per 64 KiB above. 1 GiB gets 65,536 inodes of 256 bytes, in tables set aside now: 4,096 blocks, 1.6% of the disk.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Inode tables”, 6 labelled values. This step: Inode tables: 31.5%. New in this step: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; One inode per: 16 KiB; Inodes: 65,536; and 3 more.

steps.title: The journal is 32 MiB, 62.9% of the metadata
steps.line: It doubles with disk size from 16 MiB to 1 GiB; here 3.1% of the disk.
steps.caption: mke2fs sizes the journal in steps of disk size, doubling from 16 MiB at 128 MiB to 1 GiB at 128 GiB, and no larger after that. 1 GiB gets 8,192 blocks, 32 MiB: 62.9% of the metadata and 3.1% of the disk.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Journal by disk size”, 7 labelled values. This step: Journal: 62.9%; 1 GiB: From 1 GiB: 32 MiB. New in this step: “Journal by disk size”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: The other 731 blocks: copies, bitmaps and the first files
steps.line: Superblock copies in 5 of 8 groups; two bitmaps in every group.
steps.caption: Group 0, group 1 and groups that are powers of 3, 5 or 7 keep a copy of the superblock and group descriptors: 5 of 8 groups, each with 127 spare descriptor blocks for growing the filesystem. Every group has two bitmaps. The root directory, lost+found, the orphan file and an index block take 70 blocks.
steps.picture: Pie chart “The 13,019 metadata blocks”: 3 slices; “Other metadata”, 7 labelled values. This step: Other metadata: 5.6%. New in this step: “Other metadata”, 7 labelled values.

steps.title: The default 5% reserve is 13,107 blocks, 1.0 times the metadata
steps.line: The kernel holds back 4,096 more blocks; both come out of free blocks.
steps.caption: Without -m, mke2fs reserves 5% of the blocks for root: 13,107. Its manual gives two reasons: less fragmentation, and root’s daemons keep working after other users are stopped. Once mounted, the kernel holds back 4,096 more blocks. Both come out of the free blocks.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 1 GiB”: 4 slices; “Reserves”, 5 labelled values. This step: Root reserve: 5.0%.

steps.title: Users can write 88.5% of 1 GiB: 231,922 blocks
steps.line: statfs f_bavail: the free blocks less the root and kernel reserves.
steps.caption: A user other than root can allocate blocks until only the two reserves are left: 249,125 - 13,107 - 4,096 = 231,922. statfs on the mounted filesystem reports exactly that as f_bavail, which df shows as Avail.
steps.picture: Pie chart “Every 4 KiB block of 1 GiB”: 4 slices; “statfs f_bavail”, 5 labelled values. This step: Users can write: 88.5%. New in this step: “statfs f_bavail”, 5 labelled values.

steps.title: At -m 5, users can write 88.5%, 93.3%, 94.6% of 1 GiB, 1 TiB, 20 TiB
steps.line: Metadata falls from 5.0% to 1.7% to 0.40% of the disk as disks grow.
steps.caption: Metadata shrinks as a share of the disk, from 5.0% to 1.7% to 0.40%, because the journal stops at 1 GiB and larger disks get fewer inodes per byte. A 5% reserve grows with the disk: at 20 TiB it is 1 TiB, 12.4 times the metadata.
steps.picture: “mkfs.ext4 -m 5, shares of each disk”, 3 labelled values. This case: 1 GiB: metadata 5.0%, root reserve 5.0%, users 88.5%.

steps.title: mkfs.ext4 makes 20 TiB into 5,368,709,120 blocks of 4 KiB
